opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in terms of where the model's capability actually translates into real value for people. In the early stage, a lot of us optimized for benchmarks, because they were easy to measure. But a benchmark score doesn't necessarily mean the model is useful in the scenarios people care about most.

So when I think about prioritization, I ask a few questions. First, what are the tasks where, if the model gets meaningfully better, people's productivity or experience changes a lot? Coding is a very clear example. Agentic tasks, where the model plans, uses tools, and carries a task to completion, are another. In these scenarios, going from "sometimes works" to "reliably works" is a qualitative jump, not just an incremental one.

Second, I look at whether the scenario forces the model to develop more general abilities. High-value scenarios are often hard ones, like long-horizon reasoning, dealing with real environments, and recovering from mistakes. If you train the model to do well there, the capability tends to transfer. So prioritizing them is about value, and also about pushing the model's intelligence in the right direction.

Third, resources are limited. Compute, data, and people are all finite, especially for a team that isn't the biggest in the world. You can't do everything, so you have to be honest about where you can make a real difference instead of spreading yourself thin chasing every leaderboard.

And finally, I think you have to stay close to real usage. The most valuable scenarios are often not the ones that look most impressive in a demo. They're the ones where users come back every day. Feedback from that real usage should shape what we work on next, rather than us deciding in isolation what "should" matter.

r001.rationale: The response mentions limited compute, data, and people, but does not say higher-value tasks consume more tokens.

r002.rationale: The response does not argue that AI agents need only replace the intelligence of the most intellectually capable group.

r003.rationale: It recommends prioritizing hard, high-value scenarios because success there can transfer to other tasks and push model intelligence in the right direction.

r004.rationale: The response does not present making model intelligence accessible to everyone as an approach to society-wide benefit.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest's response directly.

Thank you for having me. This is actually a question I think about almost every day, because when you're building models with limited compute and limited people, prioritization is the whole game.

The way I frame it is: where does an improvement in capability translate into a disproportionate increase in value for users? Not every capability is equal. Making a model a bit better at casual chit-chat is nice, but it doesn't change anyone's life. Making it substantially better at coding, at mathematical reasoning, at working through long, structured problems, that compounds. A developer who gets a reliable coding assistant saves hours every day, and those hours turn into products, into research, into more value downstream. So I tend to look for scenarios where the model becomes a genuine productivity multiplier rather than a novelty.

The second lens is difficulty and defensibility. Easy scenarios get commoditized very quickly. If something can be done by many teams with a modest model, there's little point in us pouring our best resources into it. Hard problems, like deep reasoning or long-horizon tasks, are where real differentiation lives, and they're also where you learn the most about the model itself. When you push on reasoning, you discover weaknesses in data, in training recipes, in evaluation, and fixing those tends to lift everything else too.

The third thing I'd say is that you have to be honest about measurability. A high-value scenario that you can't measure well is a trap, because you'll convince yourself you're making progress when you're not. So part of prioritizing is building evaluations that reflect what users actually care about, not just leaderboard numbers. Sometimes we've chosen to invest in a direction partly because we could build a clean signal for it, and that signal lets the whole team iterate fast.

And finally, I try to keep some room for bets that don't look high-value yet. The most important scenarios two years from now are probably ones we underestimate today. So most of the effort goes to the clearly valuable, clearly hard problems, but a slice is reserved for exploring things that might become the next big scenario.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what makes a scenario high-value? It’s not necessarily the one with the most users or the most impressive demo. It’s one where improving the model’s capabilities would make a meaningful difference to the task someone is trying to complete.

I would look at three things: how important the problem is, whether the current bottleneck is actually model capability, and whether we can reliably evaluate improvement. A scenario can be commercially attractive, but if the main obstacle is the workflow or access to data, training a stronger model may not solve it.

Then I’d ask whether solving that problem develops a capability that transfers to other tasks. If several valuable scenarios depend on better reasoning, for example, that gives us a stronger reason to prioritize reasoning over a narrow optimization for one application.

So I see it as a feedback loop: use real scenarios to identify weaknesses, improve the underlying capabilities, and then check whether those improvements actually help users complete their work. That last step matters—better benchmark results alone don’t establish that we’ve created more value.

r003.rationale: It gives criteria for identifying valuable scenarios to guide model capability improvements, and says to prioritize capabilities that transfer across several valuable scenarios.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is to ask what problem we’re actually solving and how much better AI can make the outcome. A technically impressive capability doesn’t automatically translate into value for users.

I’d look at three things: how important the problem is, how frequently people encounter it, and whether the model can solve it reliably enough to be useful. A scenario might have enormous potential, but if mistakes are costly and we can’t control them, it may not be the right place to start.

Then I’d build a feedback loop with real users. Start with a focused task, measure whether it saves time or improves quality, and use the failures to guide model development. That helps us prioritize capabilities based on actual needs rather than simply chasing benchmark scores.
